hints: Focus on what Group 2 nitrates always do when heated strongly, think metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen.
Remember this salt is hydrated, so its water of crystallisation must also be released as steam on strong heating.
Compare the nitrogen-containing gas actually formed, brown $\text{NO}_2$, with the nitrogen oxide named in the list and spot the odd one out.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Group 2 nitrate pattern**

Magnesium is in Group 2, so its nitrate decomposes on heating to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. This is the standard pattern for all Group 2 nitrates except the very stable barium case which needs higher temperature.

$$2\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2(\text{s}) \rightarrow 2\text{MgO(s)} + 4\text{NO}_2(\text{g}) + \text{O}_2(\text{g})$$

**Add the effect of being hydrated**

Here we have hydrated magnesium nitrate, $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. On heating, the $6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is driven off as steam, $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$.

$$\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O(s)} \rightarrow \text{MgO(s)} + 2\text{NO}_2(\text{g}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O(g})$$

**Identify the substance that does not fit**

The real products are therefore magnesium oxide, nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$), oxygen and steam. Dinitrogen monoxide, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, is a different oxide of nitrogen with nitrogen in a much lower oxidation state and is not formed here.

options.A: Dinitrogen monoxide, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, is not formed. The nitrogen product from nitrate decomposition is nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$, where nitrogen stays at +4, not +1 as in $\text{N}_2\text{O}$. So this is the correct 'will not be a product' choice.
options.B: Magnesium oxide, $\text{MgO}$, is formed as the solid residue. Students sometimes think only gases form, but the metal oxide always remains for Group 2 nitrates.
options.C: Oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, is formed alongside $\text{NO}_2$. It comes from breakdown of the nitrate ion, so do not confuse this with decomposition of a carbonate which gives only $\text{CO}_2$.
options.D: Steam, $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$, is formed because the starting solid is hydrated. The water of crystallisation is released as vapour on heating, a detail students often forget when they only recall the anhydrous equation.
